Curious how folks feel about this one now? I think a child img element (with an optional picture element parent) would give authors a great deal of flexibility in pairing poster images with video sources, and it would work quite a bit like sources already work in video when they override the src attribute (this time for poster).

I'm in favor of anything that will allow us to match the poster image with the video source 🚀 The only con I can see is that this will require repeating source elements with the media attribute (and potentially sizes, if [srcset is supported for video](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10379)). I think the added versatility is worth it though. Hi all. My team at @Squarespace has begun exploring potential spec revisions, platform tests, and browser implementations with hopes to nudge this idea along. We’re optimistic that adding the ability to use a child `` element (along with an optional `` element wrapper) to control the a `
@dalecurtis

This all seems pretty complicated, but I'm not really up to speed on the developer needs here. Can you help me understand why something like a `posterSrcSet` and `alt` attribute (https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11080 I think?) wouldn't be sufficient? 

Just adding a new attribute is pretty established, but changing what's within the `<video>` element is potentially a breaking change since that has historically been ignored (modulo `<source>` elements)

Hi @dalecurtis. Thanks for chiming in. 

> Can you help me understand why something like a posterSrcSet and alt attribute (https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11080 I think?) support wouldn't be sufficient?

I'll give it a shot!

- **Postersrcset**: Something like a `postersrcset` attribute (with a complementary `postersizes` attribute) could offer resolution switching of the same poster image at different sizes and screen densities. That would be an improvement compared to what we have today, but just as srcset is inadequate for addressing all of the scenarios that responsive images demand, postersrcset alone would be inadequate for fully pairing posters with _responsive_ video sources. In the current spec/implementations, each `video` `<source>` element can have a `media` attribute to specify the conditions where its `src` should be selected. These conditions could be things like `orientation: portrait` or `orientation: landscape` for example, to serve vertical or horizontal videos, or other media type and queries that lead to different art-directed crops of a video. Since srcset behaves more like a list of potential images that the UA can select from, it can't help authors looking to pair a specific poster image with an art directed video source. Img and picture address all of those use cases.
- **alt**: My understanding is a video itself already has various means and patterns for exposing its content with text alternatives, but a video's poster frame doesn't. Since the poster frame often acts like a title slide, sometimes with text burned into it, it would be meaningful to describe it independently of the video. If we went with an attribute for this, maybe `posteralt` might be clearer to note that it's about the poster and not the video? Not sure! At any rate, a new attribute could serve the purpose of poster alt as well as a child img could, I think. Fair point.

Having said all of that, supporting a descendent `img` (and its optional `picture` parent) could address all of these situations by reusing these elements' existing functionality, and in the process video posters could gain support for more features that are built into img elements too: like `crossorigin` `referrerpolicy` `fetchpriority` and `decoding`. Presumably, some of these could be desirable for the poster image–even independently of the video src. 

As for the breaking change concern, the spec currently mentions that other elements can be inside a video element as "fallback" content for browsers that don't understand the video element. Video-supporting browsers today ignore these elements. I think that works to the benefit of this proposal because existing browser implementations will ignore an img inside a video, while newer ones could treat it as a poster controller. A safe progressive enhancement.

Thanks for considering!

Thanks! I don't follow the `orientation` example though. AFAIK the media queries on the video source element function the same as they would on any image elements. It seems that setting the right media queries on both the `posterSizes` and source elements, would do the right thing. Are you talking about cases where source children may actually differ in content rather than just resolution or orientation? I'm not sure video has any official ways to support alt-text, but you can put a `

` tag inside the element. I think I could be convinced an img/picture as a child of the media element is useful, but the controller and complex interactions between the video and lazy loading, etc, I have a harder time understanding the use cases for. Just the child element plus some attribute on the media element (`posterchild`?), which controls activation seems sufficient.

@dalecurtis I'll try to answer using some examples. Here's a video with different sources at different breakpoints. For example sake, let's say they're not just the same video exported at different resolutions, but actually different crops or reformatted edits of a source video, with different aspect-ratios (eg wide, standard, square) designed to pair with the page layout and design of a given responsive breakpoint. ``` ``` Today's poster attribute can at-best pair an image with one of the aspect ratio/crops, but not all three. It might seem like a poster-specific version of srcset and sizes could provide the targeting to pair poster images with each breakpoint, but srcset and sizes aren't meant to be relied upon for being prescriptive with source selection like media queries are, and can result in a mismatch even if the same media conditions are used. To be clear, they could be useful for serving posters for the same video at different resolutions, which is great, but they can't suit the art directed sort of situation above. Srcset/Sizes has support for media conditions, but they're meant to be mere factors in source selection, deferring to the browser to pick one based on broader conditions it deems relevant... which could be effective connection speed, having a candidate source already in cache, screen density that best matches a given source. As one example, if you're resizing a window from large to small, a browser is allowed to keep a higher res srcset image that it already has downloaded instead of fetching a new one that matches a new narrow viewport. It can do that because they're meant to be sizes of the same image. So in the example above, a poster version of srcset and sizes would allow the browser to use a different size if it seems appropriate, which might mean the smallest image if the connection's slow, even on a wide screen. On the other hand, when we encounter these cases with image elements, we can wrap the img in a `` element to get source[media] precision instead of relying on srcset's suggestions. It comes down to whether art direction is needed. A similar situation could be described with an orientation media query, but the story is probably the same as above: you'd want to be able to prescribe a match rather than offer potential sizes. > a `

` tag inside the element. As I understand it, `video > p` is an example of fallback content that video-supporting browsers don't surface to the user unless they need to show fallback content- it isn't exposed in the accessibility tree (_a quick check in chrome a11y panel seems to confirm it's not surfaced_). My understanding is an img is similarly allowed as a video fallback element for old browsers (very old at this point), but similarly not surfaced to users today. > I think I could be convinced an img/picture as a child of the media element is useful, but the controller and complex interactions between the video and lazy loading, etc, I have a harder time understanding the use cases for I hope this helped clarify some advantages that an img element (with existing srcset/sizes support), and picture (with media query pairings) could bring for pairing responsive poster candidates either loosely or prescriptively, depending on the needs. And again, the img brings a few other features to poster like fetchpriority for resource priorities, cors control, etc that would be new to poster too.

Can you explain why not individual `poster`/`postersrcset`/`posteralt` on each `` element as per https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10378#issuecomment-4168927920 ? This is an established pattern to override the `width`/`height` attributes for `` for example (falling back to the `` attributes if not present). So to me it would make sense to allow overrides to `poster` attributes in a similar way. Along with any new attributes like `postersrcset`/`posteralt`. That seems like less of a breaking change. And, since you wouldn't need to duplicate the media attributes, this alternative may well be easier for a developer to manage. Also it could mean the browser always flips the poster image or video together — which might not be guaranteed if they are different elements (especially if the media queries get unaligned for some reason), though I guess `srcset`s can still be slightly different.

Thanks @tunetheweb That's a good one to circle back to for comparison now. First, I agree the two approaches could end up with similar in outcomes for authors. I think you're right to point out that by adding support for those new attributes on `source` elements, the poster and video source variations could share media conditions and reduce some repetition. It's here that I want to note that @dalecurtis was likely referring to this same cascade of `source[postersrcset]` usage paired with each source's media query, and if so, I'm sorry to have missed that detail Dale, as it makes the new-attributes approach a more comparable alternative! Of course, it's common for `video` elements to use a single src attribute pointing an adaptive streaming video source as well, and in those cases a video typically has no source elements at all. Those videos would still benefit from responsive (srcset-style) poster images, but their definitions would need to be on the video element itself. So I think the "add new attributes" option would need to apply to both the video element and source elements to meet the common use cases. In all, if video and source elements (strictly within video) gained support for `postersizes`, `postersrcset`, and `posteralt`, with source element values overriding the video element, I think we could have a roughly equivalent outcome to the child img poster controller approach. Great to consider. That said, the child img approach has some unique benefits to still consider before we abandon it, and it too would support the most common use cases mentioned above pretty elegantly on its own. For example, responsive poster images for the "HLS" stream single-src video markup might look something like this: ``, which seems intuitive and about the same code weight as new attributes would be. Further, from a feature comparison perspective, the child img brings built-in control over cors and fetchpriority to video poster images that wouldn't be covered by adding these 3 attributes to video and source alone. Say you have a video element that is your LCP element: being able to set `fetchpriority=high` on its poster image would be a new novel practice this would enable, and would follow current recommendations for image-based LCPs. For authors, there's also the benefit of using elements folks already know vs learning about attributes. From a spec and implementation perspective, it'd take some tinkering on both approaches to see how they compare in complexity. We've been working on spec drafts and prototypes for the img controller option, and the changes do seem to be pretty lightweight because they lean on composable existing element behavior without adding much that is new. On the other hand, my guess would be that adding 3 new attributes to both the video element and to source elements (strictly inside video elements, but not all source elements, as audio doesn't have a concept of poster to support) could mean a more complicated spec addition. I'm not sure what it would look like from a browser implementation perspective to add srcset and sizes and alt support to these two elements (perhaps there are shared conventions to make it reasonable). Lastly, there's the accessibility comparison to consider. Existing img alt surfaces on its own to the accessibility tree with no new work or challenges, while a new posteralt would take some new spec and a11y implementation thinking. I can't speak to the work involved in adding that without digging into it a bit. It seems it'd be more work than using img[alt] as it is. So I think overall this debate comes down to whether we'd prefer to bless a composable pattern of existing HTML elements or add new attributes to the language. I see benefits to both (primarily in the art directed responsive video having a little less repetition with the attributes approach), but I still think I prefer the img approach for many reasons listed above. Either way, it's great to see this moving towards some workable possibilities. That's the goal here :)

> I'm sorry to have missed that detail Dale, as it makes the new-attributes approach a more comparable alternative! No apology needed, I was indeed thinking of a single poster attribute, not the source based version since I'm unsure how that would work when we fall between sources, prior to the first frame, for non media-query reasons. The per-source version does seem much simpler and avoid duplication. > Of course, it's common for video elements to use a single src attribute pointing an adaptive streaming video source as well, Would allowing the same set of attributes on the video element itself resolve this case? > That said, the child img approach has some unique benefits... That's a good distinction. I'd expect the most common "art directed" responsive video use case to call for poster images that pair with the video source media queries, which both approaches can support (approach 2 more concisely). That said, approach 1 is the only one that would allow for decoupling the poster art direction from video sources when desirable, and that might actually be useful.

For example, if you have a video with one video source url, yet you'd like to have a responsively art-directed poster image (perhaps changing the crop of the poster image for small viewports) then Approach 1 makes that straight-forward, while Approach 2 could only pull it off by repeating the same video src in multiple source elements with different media queries and postersrc attributes.

Given that `currentPoster` enables feature testing, I think it's worth reconsidering using `poster=""` as the trigger. That seems a lot more attractive than `posterfromimg=""`.

> Given that `currentPoster` enables feature testing, I think it's worth reconsidering using `poster=""` as the trigger. That seems a lot more attractive than `posterfromimg=""`.

Yea that would be better. I think several people including myself made such comments in the past but we went with the declarative feature detection, which is perhaps not that important.

> Given that `currentPoster` enables feature testing, I think it's worth reconsidering using `poster=""` as the trigger. That seems a lot more attractive than `posterfromimg=""`.

I appreciate that `poster=""` would reuse the existing attribute, but I disagree that this would be a better trigger. If we require `poster=""` as our opt-in to using a child `img` for the poster, we will break poster image support in browsers that do not yet support the child `img` poster pattern.

For reasons beyond backwards compat too, I think it makes sense to use the poster attribute as a video's initial poster image src, giving the browser a fallback when a child img is present that doesn't have a currentSrc to use.

If we want to reconsider needing a `posterfromimg` attribute trigger at all, perhaps someone could query the httparchive for instances of `video[poster] > img` and `video > img`? Maybe we'd find that the fallback `img` pattern in `video` isn't common after all, or that the presence of a poster attribute–populated or empty–is enough of a trigger for us to use a child img as poster.

Regardless, I think it's important that we keep the poster attribute functional and allow child imgs to override it. `Posterfromimg` is a safe way to opt into that.

@scottjehl right, a polyfill like that would be needed until it's widely supported (or you could do it the other way and let the script set `poster = ""` if `currentPoster` is supported and there's an `img` or `picture` child).

As for (B), my conclusion in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/6636#issuecomment-2609956936 was that there's too much content that would start showing a (possibly bogus or unexpected) poster image without any opt-in.

On today's WHATWG call, @zcorpan offered a nice example of why some sort of opt-in will be necessary for using a child `img` as poster: many sites have used `video > img` elements to deliver a fallback image that says "your browser does not support video". We do not want those images to be used as a poster, so an opt-in is clearly necessary. In the thread above, we've been discussing two approaches to opting-into using a child poster `img`: Approach A below is currently [in our spec proposal](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12585), while approach B is a simpler alternative to consider. Either approach will work as an opt-in to enable responsive images and alt text support, and both offer browsers a trigger for looking inside a video element for an img to load during preload scanning, so we just need to work out which we prefer. I'll try and summarize the pros & cons of each approach so we can make a decision and update the proposal if needed. **A) A new `posterfromimg` boolean attribute on the `video`** ``` html ``` Pros: - compatibility: allows the poster attribute to continue referencing an image that unsupported browsers understand - clear in intention (no chance of false opt-in) Cons: - adds a new boolean attribute to the `video` element - more verbose **B) An empty `poster` attribute on the `video`** ``` html ``` Pros: - less verbose - does not require adding a new attribute to the `video` element Cons: - unsupported browsers will not load a poster image unless authors include [a JavaScript polyfill to set the video's poster property](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10378#issuecomment-5604771396)) - Some (very few) existing websites will display an image as a poster that was never intended to be used as a poster, because they currently serve an empty `poster=""` attribute with a fallback img inside the video element. This is the case the opt-in was meant to prevent. - unsupported browsers will not load a poster image if javascript fails to run or is unavailable, etc. If I missed any pros or cons, let me know and I'll update this. It shouldn't be. The hook needed already exists: media elements have a blocked-on-parser flag that's cleared when the element is popped off the stack of open elements, and [text track processing waits on it](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#text-track-model:~:text=is%20in%2E-,When,false). Waiting for `</video>` before fetching the `poster` attribute would work the same way.

I think consistency and the long-term impact of attribute vs element should weigh more than verbosity or spec effort. AFAICT there's no precedent for a boolean attribute that gives a child element a different role. HTML has `legend`, `summary` and `figcaption` rather than `<fieldset haslegend>`, `<details hassummary>` and `<figure hasfigcaption>`.
